label: Long car trip

what_happens.title: What happens on a long car trip
goals: A long trip has driving, stops and arriving
Stops are for toilets, food and stretching
The map shows how far is left
what_happens.parentSkill: Draw the trip as a line with stops, so your child can tick each one.

who_is_there.title: Who is on the trip
goals: The driver focuses on the road
Passengers help keep the car calm
Other travellers share the road and the rest stops
who_is_there.parentSkill: Explain that the driver needs to concentrate, and name another grown-up or a signal for help.

what_i_do.title: What I do in the car
goals: Use the busy bag and car games
Ask for stops and say if I feel sick
what_i_do.parentSkill: Pack small surprises to open at each stop.

if_scared.title: If the trip feels long
goals: Feeling bored or cranky is normal
Carsickness can happen and has fixes
Calm tools: stops, window, music, slow breaths
if_scared.parentSkill: Acknowledge it: 'It feels long. Two more stops, then Granny's house.'

rehearsal.title: Let's get ready for the trip
goals: Draw the trip map with stops
rehearsal.parentSkill: Let your child choose what goes in the busy bag and draw the trip map.

steps: Pack a busy bag with snacks, toys and a pillow
Buckle into the car seat or seatbelt
Drive on big roads for a long time
Stop for toilet, food and stretching at rest stops
Play car games, listen to music or nap
Watch the map to see how far is left
Arrive, stretch and explore the new place
sensory: the hum of the car and the road
trees, fields and trucks going past the window
a wobbly tummy on curvy roads
honestyNotes: Long trips can be boring, uncomfortable and sometimes make children carsick; never promise it will be quick or that they will not feel sick. Traffic can make trips longer. Use stops and landmarks rather than hours to describe the length.

fallbackAnswer: [[GROWNUP]] will tell you how many stops there are.
We can tick each stop on the trip map.
Not yet, but every stop brings us closer.
Let's look at the map together.
Tell us straight away. We can open a window, look far away or stop.
The feeling gets better with fresh air.

questionButtons.text: What if I need the toilet?
fallbackAnswer: Say so, and we will find a rest stop.
It is good to go at every stop, even a little.
Your busy bag has things to do, and we can play car games.
Being bored for a bit is okay too.

questionButtons.text: Can I sleep in the car?
fallbackAnswer: Yes, with your seatbelt on and a pillow.
Napping makes the time pass quickly.

questionButtons.text: Why are the trucks so loud?
fallbackAnswer: Big trucks have big engines, and they rumble.
They carry food and things to shops all over the country.
The driver drives carefully, and seatbelts and car seats keep everyone safe.
That is why we stay buckled.
[[GROWNUP]] or another grown-up drives and watches the road.
A grown-up is always in the car with you.

questionButtons.text: Who are all the people at the stop?
fallbackAnswer: Other families and travellers on their own trips.
You stay with us at the stop.
[[GROWNUP]] will decide the screen plan for the trip.
Looking out of the window helps if your tummy feels funny.

techniques.label: A busy bag
techniques.how: Pack books, crayons, toys and small surprises.

techniques.label: A trip map
techniques.how: Draw the route with stops to tick off.

techniques.label: Car games
techniques.how: Play I spy, counting animals or spot the colour.

techniques.label: Looking far away
techniques.how: Look at the horizon when the tummy feels wobbly.

techniques.label: Fresh air
techniques.how: Open a window a little for cool air.

techniques.label: Stop and stretch
techniques.how: Run and stretch at every rest stop.

techniques.label: Stay close at stops
techniques.how: Hold hands in car parks and stay together at stops.

techniques.label: A trip playlist
techniques.how: Let your child choose songs and stories.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

strangers: Other families are on trips too.

separation: I'm right here in the car with you.

unknown: Two more stops, then we arrive.

safety: Hold my hand in the car park.
love: I love going on adventures with you.
I'm proud of how well you are doing.

sentences.text: Soon [[CHILD]] will go on a long car trip.
First [[CHILD]] packs a busy bag with toys, books and snacks.
Then everyone buckles in, click.
Next the car drives on big roads for a long time.
Before bed, here is a story about a young badger called Bix.
Bix's family was driving to see Granny Badger by the sea.
First Bix packed a bag with a book, crayons and crackers.
Then everyone buckled in, click, click, click.
The car hummed along the long grey road.
Bix counted red cars, one, two, three.
Next they stopped at a rest stop for the toilet and a stretch.
Bix ran in circles on the grass.
Then more driving, and Bix had a little nap.
When Bix woke up, Papa said, look, the sea.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
After a while, there is a stop for the toilet, a snack and a stretch.
Then more driving, with music, games and maybe a nap.
The map shows how far is left.
Last, the car arrives, and everyone stretches and explores.
[[CHILD]] can tick each stop on the trip map.

In the story, Papa Badger drove the car.
Mama Badger sat next to him with the map.
Bix and baby sister sat in the back.
Papa needs to watch the road, said Mama, so let's keep voices calm.
Bix whispered a song to his sister.
Big trucks rumbled past, and a bus full of beavers waved.
At the rest stop, a family of rabbits was having a picnic.
Where are you going, asked a little rabbit.
To see my granny, said Bix.
Me too, said the rabbit.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.

Everyone takes turns at the toilets.
At the end, family or friends may be waiting.

Long drives are planned around distance, fuel, rest stops and traffic.
Drivers need breaks every couple of hours to stay alert, so stops keep everyone safe.
Navigation apps estimate the time, but traffic and weather can change it.
Watching the route on a map shows the towns and rivers you pass.
[[CHILD]] can be the navigator and announce the next stop.
Distracting a driver is a real safety risk, which is why calm passengers matter.
Rest stops have toilets, food and space to walk, and they are used by thousands of travellers.
Truck drivers often drive all day for work.
Families sometimes take turns driving on long trips.
[[CHILD]] can be in charge of the music playlist.
Carsickness happens when the eyes and the inner ear send different messages about movement.
Looking at the horizon, fresh air and not reading help match the signals.
Light snacks are better than big meals before a drive.
Screens can make carsickness worse for some kids.
[[CHILD]] can keep a trip journal of things spotted out of the window.
Boredom is uncomfortable but harmless, and it often leads to creative ideas.
Hunger, thirst and tiredness make crankiness worse, so check those first.
Carsickness fades once the car stops, and fresh air helps quickly.
Breaking the trip into chunks between stops makes it feel shorter.
[[CHILD]] can plan one activity for each chunk of the drive.
Planning a trip means checking the route, the stops and how long each part takes.
Downloading songs and stories before leaving avoids signal problems.
A small reward at each stop keeps morale high.
Knowing the plan reduces the, are we there yet, feeling.
[[CHILD]] can calculate how many stops there are and mark them as they go.
